Chapter 8: Healing Old Wounds — Forgiveness and Self-Compassion.
You know, as you start putting these agreements into practice, something surprising often happens. Old wounds—the kind you thought you’d buried long ago—can suddenly surface. Memories from the past... maybe a sharp comment from a teacher, a friend’s betrayal, or a moment when you felt let down by a parent. These moments, even after years, can come back with a sting that feels just as fresh as the day it happened.
I want you to picture someone who’s been working with the agreements for months. Out of nowhere, she’s hit with a childhood memory—a harsh word here, disappointment there. For so long, she tried to move on and forget. But now, it’s all right there, asking for her attention.
And honestly, most of us are carrying these old wounds quietly. They shape what we believe about ourselves—what we think is possible, what we feel we deserve, even what we think is safe. The agreements don’t ask us to ignore this pain. Instead, they invite us to meet it head-on, with honesty and a little compassion.
Let’s talk about forgiveness for a second. It’s a word that can feel impossible, right? A lot of people think it means excusing what happened, or pretending it didn’t hurt. But real forgiveness isn’t about that at all. It’s about letting go of the urge to punish—whether that’s someone else, or even yourself. It’s about loosening the grip those old stories have on you, so you can make space for something new.
I remember hearing from a parent who’d been haunted by mistakes she made years ago. She shared that the agreements helped her start forgiving herself. She realized—hey, she’d actually been doing her best, even when it wasn’t perfect. That old, critical voice—“You should have known better”—began to fade. And a new, gentler one took its place: “You did what you could. And now, you get to choose differently.”
That’s really the heart of healing—self-compassion. Most of us are quick to offer kindness to others, but when it comes to ourselves? We can be our own toughest critics. The agreements nudge us toward a different way: to speak kindly to ourselves, to show some understanding, and to remember—we’re all learning as we go.
Now, this isn’t about avoiding responsibility or skipping out on growth. It’s about seeing that pain and mistakes are just part of being human. The old wounds might not ever fully disappear, but they can lose their hold on you. Over time, those stories of failure and shame can be rewritten—turned into stories of resilience, even hope.
Healing takes time. There will be days when the pain feels just as strong as ever. But every single time you meet it with compassion, its grip loosens a little more. The journey becomes less about running from pain, and more about living fully—with all the messiness, and all the beauty, that comes with it.
